name: Preventive control
definition: Reduces the chance that an unwanted event succeeds.
example: Require a badge to unlock the server room.

name: Detective control
definition: Identifies and reports activity that has already occurred or is in progress.
example: Alert when a privileged account signs in at an unusual time.

name: Compensating control
definition: Provides comparable protection when the preferred control cannot be implemented.
example: Place a legacy system behind a tightly restricted gateway when it cannot support the required access policy itself.

name: CIA triad
definition: The three security goals are confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
example: Limit who can view a record, detect unauthorized edits, and keep the record accessible to authorized users.

name: Authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA)
definition: Verify identity, determine allowed actions, and record activity.
example: A remote-access system checks a login, applies a role, and records the session start.

name: Zero Trust
definition: Evaluate each access request using identity and context, with narrowly scoped permissions.
example: Check device compliance and user identity even when the request comes from the office network.

name: Backout plan
definition: Defines how to restore the previous state if a change fails or creates unexpected impact.
example: Restore the last working firewall configuration if a new policy blocks an approved connection.

name: Change approval
definition: Requires accountable stakeholders to review the impact, timing, risk, and recovery plan before implementation.
example: Have the service owner approve an update after the test evidence and maintenance window are reviewed.

name: Change documentation
definition: Records the approved work and updates the diagrams, procedures, and settings that describe the new state.
example: Revise the network diagram and support runbook after moving a service to another subnet.

name: Digital signature
definition: Uses a private key to sign and the corresponding public key to verify integrity and signer identity when the key is trusted.
example: Verify the signature on a software update before installing it.

name: Password salt
definition: A unique random value stored with each password hash that prevents identical passwords from producing identical stored hashes.
example: Two users choose the same password, but their stored hashes differ because their salts differ.

name: Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP)
definition: Lets a client check the revocation status of a particular certificate.
example: A client checks whether a certificate was revoked after the associated private key was exposed.

name: Insider threat
definition: Risk from someone with existing trusted access, including deliberate misuse and harmful mistakes.
example: A contractor accidentally shares restricted data with an unauthorized recipient.

name: Nation-state actor
definition: A government-backed group commonly associated with strategic goals such as espionage or disruption.
example: Investigators consider possible state sponsorship after a sustained campaign against strategic research organizations.

name: Organized crime
definition: A coordinated group typically motivated by financial gain.
example: A criminal group demands payment after disrupting a business with ransomware.

name: Smishing
definition: Social engineering delivered through text messages.
example: An unexpected text claims a delivery is delayed and requests payment through a link.

name: Business email compromise (BEC)
definition: Uses a trusted business identity or account to induce an unauthorized action, often a transfer of funds.
example: A supposed supplier asks accounts payable to change bank details, which the team verifies using its established phone number.

name: Supply chain threat vector
definition: Uses a trusted supplier, dependency, or distribution channel to reach an organization.
example: An organization reviews its exposure after a vendor announces that an update package was compromised.

name: Zero-day vulnerability
definition: A weakness for which an effective vendor fix is unavailable at the time it is first disclosed or used.
example: A vendor issues temporary mitigations while it develops a patch for a newly reported flaw.

name: Race condition
definition: A flaw in which security depends on operations occurring in a particular order or within a timing window.
example: A code review finds that a resource can change between its permission check and its use.

name: Cloud misconfiguration
definition: A cloud setting that grants more access or exposure than intended.
example: A security review identifies a storage bucket that permits public reads despite holding internal files.

name: Password spraying
definition: An attack pattern that tries a small set of common passwords across many accounts.
example: Identity logs show a burst of failed sign-ins spread across a large number of users.

name: Ransomware indicators
definition: Unexpected widespread file modifications combined with related alerts or a ransom demand can indicate ransomware.
example: Endpoint tooling alerts on unusual file rewrites, and users report unfamiliar extensions on shared files.

name: Distributed denial of service (DDoS)
definition: Traffic or requests from many sources exhaust a service’s capacity and disrupt availability.
example: Monitoring shows a sharp increase in traffic from numerous origins alongside application timeouts.

name: Network segmentation
definition: Separates systems into zones and restricts traffic between them to limit exposure and lateral movement.
example: Guest Wi-Fi cannot reach the organization’s internal application subnet.

name: Application allowlisting
definition: Permits approved software to run and blocks execution outside the approved policy.
example: A point-of-sale device permits only the sales application and approved support tools.

name: System hardening
definition: Reduces a system’s attack surface by applying secure settings and removing unnecessary capabilities.
example: Disable unused services and remove default accounts on a server image before deployment.

name: Cloud shared responsibility
definition: Divides security duties between the cloud provider and customer, with the split depending on the service model.
example: For a cloud virtual machine, the provider protects the physical host and the customer patches the guest operating system.

name: Infrastructure as code (IaC)
definition: Describes infrastructure in version-controlled files for consistent, reviewable deployment.
example: Review changes to a network template before using it to create a new environment.

name: Containers and virtual machines
definition: Containers generally share a host kernel, while each virtual machine runs its own guest operating system.
example: An architecture review compares the isolation and management needs of shared-kernel workloads and separate guest systems.

name: Fail-open and fail-closed
definition: Fail-open permits access when a control fails. Fail-closed denies access when it cannot enforce the policy.
example: A protected application rejects access when its authorization service is unavailable.

name: IEEE 802.1X
definition: Controls access to a wired or wireless network port by authenticating a user or device.
example: A switch keeps a workstation’s network access restricted until its certificate is verified.

name: Secure Access Service Edge (SASE)
definition: Combines wide-area networking with security services commonly delivered from the cloud.
example: Apply consistent web and access policies to branch offices and remote workers.

name: Data at rest, in transit, and in use
definition: Data can be stored, moving between systems, or actively processed. Each state calls for appropriate safeguards.
example: Encrypt disks for stored data and use TLS when sending that data to another system.

name: Data classification
definition: Labels information according to sensitivity and handling requirements.
example: Classify payroll files as restricted and limit their access and sharing.

name: Data sovereignty
definition: Data is subject to applicable laws in the jurisdiction where it is stored or processed.
example: A company checks whether regional obligations affect its choice of cloud region and backup location.

name: Hot, warm, and cold recovery sites
definition: A hot site is ready to take over quickly, a warm site has partial readiness, and a cold site needs substantial setup.
example: A payment service plans for a hot site because it must resume service quickly after a disaster.

name: Offsite backup
definition: Stores a recoverable copy away from the primary site to reduce exposure to a shared physical incident.
example: Restore records from backups in a separate location after a building flood.

name: Failover testing
definition: Verifies whether a standby component can take over when the primary component is unavailable.
example: Run a controlled switch to a standby database and confirm that clients can reconnect.

name: Secure baseline
definition: An approved set of security settings used to deploy and assess a type of system.
example: Compare new laptops against the standard that specifies disk encryption and the host firewall.

name: Mobile device management (MDM)
definition: Centrally applies mobile-device settings and can enforce controls such as encryption or managed-data removal.
example: Require passcodes and block company email access from devices that fail compliance checks.

name: Static code analysis
definition: Examines source code or compiled artifacts without executing the application.
example: The build pipeline flags a potentially unsafe use of untrusted input before deployment.

name: Asset inventory
definition: Records hardware, software, or data assets and key details needed to manage them throughout their lifecycle.
example: Track a laptop’s owner, location, and lifecycle status so the team can recover it during offboarding.

name: Asset assignment
definition: Makes someone accountable for an asset and its handling throughout its lifecycle.
example: Record the application owner responsible for reviewing access and approving retirement.

name: Media sanitization
definition: Makes stored data infeasible to recover using a method appropriate to the media and its sensitivity.
example: Verify sanitization before releasing retired storage to a recycler.

name: CVSS and CVE
definition: CVSS describes vulnerability severity, while a CVE ID identifies a specific publicly cataloged vulnerability.
example: Use the CVE ID to match advisory records and combine CVSS with business impact to prioritize remediation.

name: Remediation prioritization
definition: Ranks fixes using severity, exposure, exploitability, and the importance of affected assets.
example: Patch an exposed customer portal before a similarly rated system with tightly restricted reachability.

name: Remediation validation
definition: Checks that a corrective action resolved the original finding.
example: Rescan the patched host and confirm the flagged package version is no longer installed.

name: Security information and event management (SIEM)
definition: Centralizes events and correlates records to help detect and investigate security activity.
example: Correlate a suspicious sign-in with an endpoint alert from the same user session.

name: Alert tuning
definition: Adjusts detection logic or thresholds using evidence to improve the quality of alerts.
example: Refine a rule after confirming that a known backup job repeatedly triggers benign alerts.

name: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
definition: Collects network-device metrics and notifications. SNMPv3 can add authentication and encryption.
example: Monitor a switch’s interface utilization and receive alerts for link-state changes.

name: Endpoint detection and response (EDR)
definition: Collects endpoint activity and lets responders investigate and take actions on affected systems.
example: Review a process tree and isolate a suspected compromised workstation.

name: Network access control (NAC)
definition: Enforces network admission policy using device identity, posture, or both.
example: Send a noncompliant laptop to a restricted network until its security software is updated.

name: DMARC
definition: Uses alignment with SPF or DKIM to help domain owners publish email handling policy and receive reports.
example: A mail administrator reviews reports for messages claiming to come from the company’s domain without aligned authentication.

name: Role-based and attribute-based access control
definition: RBAC uses assigned roles. ABAC evaluates attributes about the requester, resource, action, or environment.
example: Payroll staff receive permissions by role, and a separate policy also checks device compliance for sensitive records.

name: Multifactor authentication (MFA)
definition: Requires evidence from distinct factor categories such as knowledge, possession, or inherence.
example: Sign in using a password and a registered hardware security key.

name: Privileged access management (PAM)
definition: Controls and audits elevated access using measures such as credential vaulting and time-limited privilege.
example: Grant an administrator just-in-time access for an approved maintenance task and record its use.

name: Security orchestration
definition: Coordinates multiple tools and actions into a repeatable workflow.
example: A verified alert triggers enrichment, opens a ticket, and requests analyst approval for isolation.

name: Guardrails for automation
definition: Set limits and safety checks on what automated workflows can do.
example: Require human approval before automated containment can affect a production server.

name: Automated provisioning
definition: Uses approved workflows and standard settings to create or update accounts or infrastructure consistently.
example: Create new employee accounts with approved role assignments after onboarding approval.

name: Containment
definition: Limits an incident’s spread while investigation and recovery continue.
example: Isolate a workstation from the network after confirming suspicious activity.

name: Chain of custody
definition: Documents who collected, handled, transferred, or stored evidence and when.
example: Record each transfer of a forensic copy and verify the copy’s hash on receipt.

name: Lessons learned
definition: Reviews response performance and assigns improvements after an incident.
example: Update the escalation runbook after an incident review identifies delayed notifications.

name: Firewall logs
definition: Record network policy decisions and commonly include source, destination, ports, protocol, and action.
example: Check whether an outbound connection from a workstation matched a deny rule.

name: Endpoint logs
definition: Reveal activity local to a device, such as process launches, file changes, and host security events.
example: Determine which process initiated an unusual outbound connection.

name: Packet capture
definition: Records network packets for analysis of communication details visible at the capture point.
example: Compare protocol exchanges when investigating repeated connection failures.

name: Policy, standard, and procedure
definition: A policy sets direction, a standard defines required rules, and a procedure specifies how to carry out a task.
example: A policy requires data protection, a standard specifies storage encryption, and a procedure explains how to verify it.

name: Data owner and data custodian
definition: The owner decides handling and classification requirements. The custodian implements and operates safeguards.
example: The owner classifies payroll records, and the storage team enforces access and backup settings.

name: Acceptable use policy (AUP)
definition: Defines permitted and prohibited uses of organizational systems and resources.
example: Explain whether employees may install unapproved applications on company laptops.

name: Risk register
definition: Tracks identified risks, their owners, assessments, and planned responses.
example: Record a vendor outage risk, assign an owner, and track the status of a backup provider plan.

name: Annualized loss expectancy (ALE)
definition: Estimates annual loss by multiplying single loss expectancy by the annual rate of occurrence.
example: A $20,000 loss expected once every four years gives an ALE of $5,000.

name: RTO and RPO
definition: Recovery time objective is the target time to restore service. Recovery point objective is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
example: A two-hour RTO and a 15-minute RPO imply restoration within two hours using data no more than 15 minutes old at interruption.

name: Vendor due diligence
definition: Evaluates a supplier’s security posture, risks, and ability to meet requirements before engagement.
example: Review a SaaS vendor’s independent audit report and incident notification terms before sharing sensitive data.

name: Service-level agreement (SLA)
definition: Defines measurable service commitments and how performance is evaluated.
example: A contract specifies monthly uptime and the response target for urgent outages.

name: Right-to-audit clause
definition: Preserves the customer’s contractual ability to review a supplier’s compliance under agreed conditions.
example: A customer requests supporting evidence after a vendor changes a subcontractor that handles sensitive records.

name: Compliance monitoring
definition: Regularly checks and records whether controls meet applicable obligations.
example: Collect access-review evidence each quarter to demonstrate adherence to the organization’s required review schedule.

name: Privacy data inventory
definition: Records what personal data is held, where it resides, who can access it, and why it is processed.
example: Map all stores of customer contact information to support a privacy review.

name: Right to be forgotten
definition: A privacy right to request erasure where applicable, subject to legal grounds and exceptions.
example: Route a deletion request for review because some records may have a mandatory retention period.

name: Internal and external audits
definition: Internal audits are conducted on behalf of the organization. External audits are conducted by an outside party.
example: An internal team reviews control evidence before an independent assessor evaluates the same program.

name: Attestation
definition: A formal statement about whether specified controls or requirements have been met, based on evidence.
example: An independent practitioner issues a report about the design and operation of a service provider’s controls.

name: Assessment environment knowledge
definition: A known, partially known, or unknown environment describes how much system information an authorized assessment team receives in advance.
example: Providing architecture diagrams and test accounts makes the engagement more informed than supplying only a public entry point.

name: Phishing awareness exercise
definition: Uses authorized simulations and feedback to practice recognizing and reporting suspicious messages.
example: Track how often staff report simulated messages and use the results to improve training.

name: Anomalous behavior recognition
definition: Teaches staff to identify and report activity that deviates from expected patterns.
example: Report an unexpected request for a confidential export made through a new chat account.

name: Recurring security awareness training
definition: Reinforces behaviors over time and adapts to changes in organizational risk.
example: Use periodic short lessons and measure whether employees apply the approved process for reporting suspicious messages.
